notes.1a: The majority of candidates correctly identified the sections of the graph. Weaker candidates gave insufficient information such as stating “constant” when “constant speed” was required.
notes.1b: The majority of candidates attempted to use the correct equation. Stronger candidates went on to use average speed or the area under the graph.
notes.2a: The majority of candidates calculated the correct mass.
notes.2bi: Most candidates were able to read the measuring cylinder and gave the correct answer.
notes.2bii: Most candidates added the volumes correctly and gave the correct answer.
notes.2biii: The weakest candidates struggled to recall the correct formula. However, most candidates gave a good structured response resulting in the correct answer. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0625 Physics June 2019
notes.3ai: Most candidates struggled to read the stopwatches and calculate the time interval. Some added the times together. Few candidates recognised that they needed to double the time interval to calculate one complete oscillation.
notes.3aii: Only the strongest candidates answered this question correctly and many other candidates seemed unfamiliar with this experiment and how timing errors could be reduced. Many gained credit for starting the stopwatch at the same time as releasing the bob. Some went on to gain further credit for stopping the stopwatch when the bob returned to its starting point. Few suggested timing multiple swings and dividing the total time by the number of swings to get an accurate value for one swing. Many preferred instead to repeat the experiment several times for one swing and then take an average, which could not be credited.
notes.3b: The strongest candidates were able to interpret information correctly and worked out that the kinetic energy at R was 0.4 (J) and at Q was 0.0 (J).
notes.4ai: Most candidates answered this question correctly.
notes.4aii: Weaker candidates indicated that molecules would move faster. Stronger candidates went on to say that the molecules had more collisions with the walls of the balloon.
notes.4b: Most candidates gave a good structured response resulting in the correct answer. Some candidates gave Pascals as the unit, others correctly converted to Pascals.
notes.5a: Almost all candidates indicated the correct sequence for the nuclear power station.
notes.5bi: Most candidates interpreted the graph correctly.
notes.5bii: Most candidates stated that the LED required less power but very few went on to explain how this was better for the environment.
notes.6ai: Most candidates were able to identify line X as the normal.
notes.6aii: Most candidates correctly identified angle Y as the angle of incidence.
notes.6aiii: Most candidates correctly stated that angle Z would also double. Some candidates stated that Z would increase but this was not enough for credit.
notes.6bi: Many candidates correctly identified point F as the focal point but others named a length or angle.
notes.6bii: Many candidates correctly described the image as inverted, diminished and sometimes real. Others struggled to use the correct terminology resulting in confusing descriptions of the image.
notes.7a: Most candidates answered this well giving good descriptions of the arrangement of molecules in solids as closely packed, in liquids loosely packed and gases being widely spaced. Some candidates gave general descriptions of the properties of solids, liquids and gases, which did not gain credit.
notes.7bi: Most correctly identified the process as evaporation.
notes.7bii: Most candidates found describing the cooling effect of evaporation a challenge. Some described molecules with more energy escaping. Only a few were able to go on to explain how this led to a lowering of the average energy of the remaining molecules and therefore lower temperature of the liquid. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0625 Physics June 2019
notes.8ai: Most candidates correctly placed the N pole on the right and the S pole on the left of the magnet. A few incorrectly placed the poles away from the magnet in the magnetic field.
notes.8aii: Very few candidates were able to explain that the magnet induced a N pole in the iron bar next to the S pole of the magnet.
notes.8bi: Stronger candidates were able to draw an appropriate symbol for a power supply and make the correct connections to the ends of the coil.
notes.8bii: Stronger candidates correctly stated that an advantage of an electromagnet was that it can be switched on/off easily.
notes.9a: Most candidates correctly described rubbing the ruler with a cloth but few went on to describe how electrons were moved from the ruler to the cloth.
notes.9bi: Most candidates correctly identified the charge on the rod as positive.
notes.9bii: Most candidates correctly stated that same charges repel. A few were confused with magnetism and talked about poles. Some candidates stated “the ruler repels the sphere” but this was stated in the question and so could not be credited.
notes.10a: Most candidates knew the circuit symbols and were able to place them correctly in the circuit.
notes.10b: Few candidates understood that the brightness of the remaining lamp in a parallel circuit would stay the same. Most thought that the remaining lamp would get brighter. Very few were able to explain that the current through the remaining lamp would remain the same.
notes.11a: Only the strongest candidates were able to identify the transformer as a step down transformer.
notes.11b: Some of the strongest candidates were able to identify the metal core as being iron. Some went on to explain that iron was easily magnetised and demagnetised. Many incorrectly stated it was because it was a good conductor.
notes.11ci: Most of the stronger candidates were able to correctly calculate the output voltage. Others struggled to recall and use the formula correctly.
notes.11cii: Many candidates linked the number of turns to voltage but did not quantify it. Candidates who stated “the voltage is higher because the number of turns is higher” gained partial credit.
notes.12a: Many candidates were able to define “random” correctly as unpredictable. Many explanations were too vague and some candidates struggled to express themselves clearly.
notes.12b: This question was answered well with most candidates completing the table correctly.
notes.12c: Some of the strongest candidates drew a good diagram of 2 protons and 2 neutrons in a nucleus with good labelling. Many drew diagrams of an atom including electrons. Some drew good diagrams but without labels. Some wrote nuclide notation and some drew a table. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0625 Physics June 2019
